title: The fruits of Communion (CCC 1391–1401)
hook: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sin, unity, care for the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the real presence: Christ present in many ways, and above all under the bread and wine. Your line was truly, really, substantially. Did you slow down passing a church? Day one thousand one hundred.

Right after Communion, the Mass goes quiet. People file back from the front and kneel or sit. Some close their eyes. Some stare at the floor. A child swings her feet. The organist plays something soft, or nothing at all. It can look like nothing is happening. The Catechism disagrees. It lists what Communion does in a person, and the list doesn't stop at the pew. It ends somewhere unexpected: out on the street, with people who are hungry. Today, the fruits.
screen: `THE QUIET AFTER COMMUNION.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE NOTHING.` → `THE LIST ENDS ON THE STREET.`

segments.voice: The first fruit is union with Christ. The Catechism quotes Jesus in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, abideth in me, and I in him." Abiding: staying, living with. And the Catechism compares Communion to ordinary food. What bread does for the body, this does for the life of grace begun at baptism: it keeps it, grows it, renews it. The second fruit is separation from sin. The body given up for us and the blood shed for the forgiveness of sins can't unite people to Christ without also cleansing them. The Catechism says Communion strengthens charity, and that charity wipes away venial sins, the everyday ones, and helps protect against grave sin in the future. It's careful to add that Communion isn't meant for forgiving mortal sins; that belongs to the sacrament of penance. The third fruit is unity. Paul puts it in one line: "For we, being many, are one bread, one body, all that partake of one bread." So the Eucharist makes the Church. Receiving Christ's body joins people to everyone else who receives it. And the last fruit on the list is the one on the street. The Catechism says that to receive in truth the body and blood of Christ given up for us, we must recognize Christ in the poorest, his brothers and sisters. It cites John Chrysostom, who warned people who had tasted the Lord's blood against failing to recognize their own brother in need. Then, honestly, the section ends with a sorrow: Christians who can't yet share one table, and a hope that they one day will. Communion makes communion.
screen: `UNION: ABIDETH IN ME.` · `SEPARATION FROM SIN.` · `UNITY: ONE BREAD, ONE BODY.` · `THE POOR: CHRIST'S BROTHERS AND SISTERS.` · then, large: `WE, BEING MANY, ARE ONE BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give to the poor after Mass. Settle, and breathe. Think of the walk out of church, or out of your front door. Who's there? Someone asking for change. A food bank collection bin. A neighbor who's struggling and doesn't say so. Choose one concrete gift you can give today or after your next Mass: money, food, an hour, a phone call. Make it small enough that you'll really do it. Hold the person or the place in mind while you breathe. If you pray, you can bring them to the altar with you. The bell holds the time.
The fruits of Communion. Union with Christ, separation from sin, unity in one body, and care for the poor, his brothers and sisters. Today's word.
Your line: communion makes communion. Today, give the gift you chose, and give it in person if you can, with a word and a look, not just a coin. Day one thousand one hundred.

howItsDone: After receiving Communion, Catholics spend a few moments in silent thanksgiving; some parishes take up a collection for the poor at Mass or keep food bins by the church doors.

original.note: Greek: sharing, fellowship; the word in Paul's letters behind 'communion' with the body and blood of Christ.

trapdoor: what you thought: Communion is a private moment with God.
what it means: union with Christ that pulls people away from sin, into one body, and out toward the poor.
